chapter: Barry Martin and New Orleans tours to England
title: Barry Martin's start and his trip to New Orleans
summary: Background of drummer Barry Martin from Virginia Water, his early bands, Studio 51 residency, and his 1961 journey to New Orleans where he made two recordings.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: Now may I ask you, from where is Barry Martin spring?

Barry Martin spring? He's a sort of hometown boy from a place called Virginia Water. His father's family comes from a musical family. His mother sang at one time. His father, I believe, played saxophone, or he played drums or saxophone in his small dance bands for many years, and he went into the green grocery business. Barry had heard these bands of Littleton and Barber and Collier, and was duly inspired. And from about the age of fourteen, he was knocking about on drums then. He had a few local fellas around, and they used to play about a three piece band for Boy Scout dances, and our British Legion dances. He held up with Keith Smith at that time, and they were very friendly at that time. And their first little band was known as the Frondzy Me Band, was in 1958. Well, not a very popular band, but a very local band in the Surrey countryside. They used to play small jobs, carnivals and things like this. Well, late 1959, Barry had sorted out what he wanted to do and what he was going to do. Keith Smith had gone his own separate way. And Barry then had a regular band, and they had their first London job in about 1959, the Studio 51, the Ken Collier Club. And they got the residency every Wednesday. They had a Wednesday night residency there. And that was their first London job. And they never really looked back from there. Barry went about seven years without a personnel change in his band, except for the trumpet player, who never did take it very seriously and decided to retire at an early age. What was that? What was that? Clive Blackmore, who was a Kid Howard-inspired trumpet player, but he was only ever an amateur, and he was quite satisfied in the early days of doing these local jobs. But when Barry decided to broaden his outlook, then Clive went his own way, and Cuff Billet from Portsmouth joined the band. And that band stayed together for about seven years. Now, in 1961, Barry decided it was about time he found out more about it, and to come to New Orleans. He had no money at all, though I can recollect a little story. I was with Barry the night before he left for New Orleans in 19 February 1961. They were playing a job at a place called the Palm Court in Pearlie, which is now again a London suburb. It wasn't then. And Barry had exactly thirty shillings in his pocket and was due to leave for New Orleans the following morning. And he went to New Orleans via Canada and he worked in a boot factory in Canada, putting laces and shoes, and eventually this type of work. He worked in a road gang and all this type of thing. And eventually, after about eight months, arrived in New Orleans with about a thousand dollars, he'd say. While he was here, he made two recordings. At that time, he wanted a dance band sound. He recorded Kitchig Swingsters, which was a regular band at that period. And he also recorded Kid Hats.
